1 ISSUE
2
3 BRYDON, Chair --For business and occupation tax classification
4 purposes, is a Washington food processor that purchases semi -finished
5 soybean oil and canola oil in bulk and processes these oils into
6 various finished products, classified as a manufacturer of soybeans
7 into soybean oil or canola into canola oil at a rate of 0. 138 percent
8 RCW 82. 04. 260 ( 1)( a)) or classified as a general manufacturer subject
9 to a rate of 0. 484 percent ( RCW 82. 04. 240)?
10
11 The Board finds the correct classification is general manu-
12 facturer at the rate of 0. 484 percent.
13
14 FACTS AND CONTENTIONS
15
16 The parties stipulated to the facts, which. we summarize. The
17 Taxpayer purchases soybean oil and canola oil in bulk from suppliers
18 outside of Washington. The bulk oil is shipped via railway tank car
19 to the Taxpayer' s facility in Kent, Washington, where it is processed
20 into finished products for use in food preparation. The Taxpayer
21 heats the oil, adds varying ingredients, packages, and sells the
22 resultant finished products to a wholesale distributor and to end
23 users.

20 ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
21
22 We search in vain for evidence to support Taxpayer' s contention
23 that he directly purchases and has ownership of soybeans or canola
24 beans that are manufactured into the semi -finished oil that arrives by
25 railcar at his plant. The Taxpayer testified that he purchases
26

1 soybean oil and canola oil, not unrefined beans. There is evidence
2 the Taxpayer purchased soybean oil from Archer Daniels Midland Company
3 Department' s Exhibit R- 7). The Stipulation of Facts at page 1 states
4 he purchases both soybean oil and canola oil that are delivered to the
5 Taxpayer' s facility at Kent by railcar. We conclude the Taxpayer
6 purchases semi -refined soybean oil and canola oil, not soybeans or
7 canola beans.

10 ambiguous, and the Department has interpreted the statute " somewhat
11 subjectively". The Taxpayer' s notion of ambiguity is grounded in part
12 in a belief that the state has never had a soybean crop or canola
13 crop, 2 which leads him to question the purpose for providing a special
14 tax category for these unavailable agricultural products.

22 raw bean into finished products. Therefore, it should be taxed at the

9 Legislative motivation and intent underpinning the creation of
10 various tax categories are manifold. For example, if the intent is to
11 encourage development of a new agricultural crop heretofore not
12 produced in the state, one tool to signal encouragement is a favorable
13 tax rate for the desired product. This exemplifies how tax policy may
14 be used to encourage a desired economic outcome and is a credible
15 basis for establishing a tax rate for a specific product that predates
16 its production within the state --in this instance, the manufacture of
17 soybean oil and canola oil.
18

20 wide discretion in classifying business activity for purposes of
21 levying excise taxes, and the Legislature may establish unequal rates
22 and exemptions that will be upheld provided the difference rests on

some reasonable basis. Taxpayer does not directly challenge the
different tax rates levied for the process of manufacturing oil from
beans and for subsequent processes that use the oil. Rather, he
argues that all food processing should be taxed at the lower 0. 138
percent rate. We are not persuaded.
Is the language of the former RCW 82. 04. 260( 2) in any way
ambiguous?5 In pertinent part, this statute reads:
Upon every person engaging within this state in the
business of manufacturing wheat into flour, barley into
pearl barley, soybeans into soybean oil, canola into canola
oil, canola meal, canola byproducts, or sunflower seeds
into sunflower oil; as to such persons the amount of tax
with respect to such business shall be equal to the value
of the flour, pearl barley, oil, canola meal or canola
byproduct manufactured multiplied by the rate of 0. 138
percent.
Emphasis added.)
The statute is written in plain language. We find no uncertainty
of meaning in the statutory provision, and we do not find evidence of
subjectivity in the Department' s reading of the law. The special
0. 138 percent tax rate applies solely to the manufacture of soybean
oil and canola oil and not to other products subsequently manufactured
from these oils. Further, we do not discern a legislative intent in
Chapter 82 RCW that all food processing activity is encompassed within
Ambiguous - an uncertainty of meaning or intention, as in a contractual
term or statutory provision. Black' s Law Dictionary 79- 80 ( 7th ed. 1999).

1 the limited and specific food manufacturing activities described in
2 the former RCW 82. 04. 260, as contended by Taxpayer.
3
4 Taxpayer described in testimony the basic process to change
5 canola to canola oil. The beans are crushed and produce a mash
6 consisting of oil and bean husks. The mash is processed to remove the
7 husk material producing semi -refined canola oil ready for sale to
8 others who, by heating, cooling, and adding other ingredients, manu-
9 facture finished products for the marketplace. The manufacturing
10 activity of the Taxpayer is limited to those processes employed after
11 production of the soybean or canola oil. We conclude the Taxpayer
12 engages in manufacturing processes subsequent to creation of soybean
13 and canola oils. Therefore, the Taxpayer does not qualify for the
14 special tax rate of 0. 138 percent established by the former RCW
15 82. 04. 260( 2) for the manufacture of soybeans to soybean oil and canola
16 to canola oil.
17
18 We conclude Taxpayer' s manufacturing activity is correctly
19 classified under RCW 82. 04. 240 at a rate of 0. 484 percent. Deter-
20 mination No. 99- 143R is affirmed.
